verdicts.trueWording: adventures should not foster competition between the DM and players
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the prohibitive modality 'may not' — the guide says 'should not', and uses 'may not' two sentences earlier for a hard ban ('They may not cross over into other settings'), so the two registers are deliberately distinguished in the same paragraph
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched (HTTP 200, 9pp, pypdf extract). Page 1: 'While characters suffering from poor choices is certainly reasonable, adventures should not foster an atmosphere of competition between the DM and the players.*' Quote 'atmosphere of competition between the DM and' is verbatim. The trailing asterisk is the document's change-marker (see the June 2025 changelog on the last page), not a hardness marker.
Raw PDF, page 1 line 11 carries the string verbatim, including the May 2025 effective date. Both limbs (version 1.9c; updated June 23, 2025) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide (also provided)
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'so the requirement has been constant across versions' — a cross-version inference the 2021 document does not make; also 'required' overstates the page's 'You should be familiar'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched (HTTP 200, 10pp). The style-guide sentence appears twice (Option 1 and Option 2 sections); the doc also says 'you'll also want the adventure templates and style guides used for the Dungeoncraft program'. Version line: 'Effective Date: October 1, 2021. Version 1.2.' The claim carries no quote, so verbatim was not possible. Independent corroboration for the constancy limb: the v1.9c PDF fetched for claims 364/365 carries the same sentence verbatim ('You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide (also provided) as well.') — but that is my cross-check, not this page's assertion, so the limb stays unsupported at its cited source.

Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200, 120KB; full glossary body present, not gated). Quote 'Tags in Brackets.' is verbatim in the Glossary Conventions section. Every capitalization limb is demonstrated on the page: conditions ('the Prone condition', 'the Blinded condition', 'the Charmed condition', '[Condition]' tags); actions ('Attack [Action]', 'take the Dash action', 'take the Disengage action', 'take the Dodge action', 'take the Help action'); 'Hit Points'; 'Armor Class (AC)'; 'Proficiency Bonus'; 'A Long Rest is a period of extended downtime'; 'spend Hit Dice during a Short Rest'. Page is the 2024 free rules glossary (posted Sep 1, 2024).

verdicts.trueWording: a monster that has a personal name and a distinct personality
verdicts.note: All three limbs verbatim on the raw page. Creature: 'Any being in the game, including a player's character, is a creature.' Monster: 'A monster is a creature controlled by the DM, even if the creature is benevolent.' Nonplayer Character: 'A nonplayer character (NPC) is a monster that has a personal name and a distinct personality.'

verdicts.trueWording: Most player characters are of the Humanoid type.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'and species' — the word 'species' does not occur anywhere in the glossary text; its only two occurrences in the fetched page are D&D Beyond site-navigation links ('Rules Browse > Species'), which are chrome, not glossary prose
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim under the 'Creature Type' entry: 'Every creature, including every player character, has a tag in the rules that identifies the type of creature it is. Most player characters are of the Humanoid type. These are the game's creature types:' followed by Aberration/Beast/Celestial/... The 'creature types' limb and the 'avoiding race' limb both hold — a case-insensitive grep for race/races/racial over the whole 70KB extraction returns zero hits. Only the 'species' limb fails at this source.

verdicts.trueWording: careful about avoiding the common pitfalls
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200). Embedded tweet, bylined 'Jeremy Crawford (@JeremyECrawford) December 21, 2018': 'The current version of the D&D style guide permits the use of they/them as a singular pronoun, as long as the writer is careful about avoiding the common pitfalls ("Are you referring to this one person or this other group of people you also mentioned?").' Every limb holds, including the antecedent-ambiguity gloss, which the parenthetical spells out. (The Sage Advice post itself is dated January 4, 2019; the claim's 2018-12-21 is the tweet date, which is what the page shows.)

verdicts.trueWording: tips on achieving gender neutral language
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200) at the dated permalink. Embedded tweet bylined 'Dungeon Masters Guild (@dms_guild) February 22, 2019': 'An updated #DnD House Style Guide is now on #DMsGuild, creators! Among other changes, this guide includes tips on achieving gender neutral language.' 'Among other changes' is what makes 'singled out' and 'new' fair — it is the one change the tweet names. (Sage Advice post date is April 1, 2019; the claim's date is the tweet's.)

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'poll' — the page carries a plain question tweet with no poll options, no vote counts and no poll markup (a grep for 'poll' over the raw HTML returns zero hits); the embedded blockquote is only the question text plus #DnD #WOTCstaff
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200). Blockquote: 'DMs, how much boxed text (aka read-aloud text) do you like in an adventure you run? #DnD #WOTCstaff — Jeremy Crawford (@JeremyECrawford) November 17, 2016' (status 799355247135076354). Quote verbatim; Crawford and 2016 hold. A Twitter poll's options are stripped from oEmbed blockquotes, so this is not CONTRADICTED — the page simply does not support 'poll'. Second, weaker soft spot worth recording: 'the terminology WotC uses' is an inference — the page shows one WotC designer using the phrase (with a #WOTCstaff tag), not a house-style statement.

Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200). Blockquote bylined 'SlyFlourish (@SlyFlourish) April 12, 2019': 'In my own #dnd adventure writing I use boxed text, and "area aspects" which are like bullet points. I also avoid talking about living things in boxed text to avoid the whole "those orcs I mentioned aren't really there". Brevity is critically important as well.' Quote verbatim; the living-things limb and its reason are both explicit. Recorded, not graded down: the page bylines the handle @SlyFlourish and never prints the name 'Mike Shea'. I treat handle-to-person resolution as naming the same account holder, not as an added assertion — unlike claim 374, where the claim adds a credential the page does not carry. Second minor: Shea states it as his own practice ('In my own adventure writing I... avoid'), which the claim generalizes to 'should be kept out'.

verdicts.trueWording: too long (anything over a paragraph or so)
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'AL administrator' — the page gives Greg Marks no role, title or affiliation; it bylines him only as 'Greg Marks (@Skerrit7h3green)'. The credential is load-bearing here, because the surrounding claims lean on Adventurers League authority
verdicts.note: Same raw page as 373/375. Blockquote bylined 'Greg Marks (@Skerrit7h3green) April 15, 2019': 'However, I also think lots of boxed text is unnecessary (an empty room doesn't need boxed text), too long (anything over a paragraph or so), written poorly burying important details, pretends to be a story to be listened to by the players, preventing them from being involved.' Quote 'a paragraph or so' verbatim; the length-ceiling criticism is fully supported. Only the AL-administrator credential fails.

verdicts.trueWording: A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Blockquote bylined 'Shawn Merwin (or a poor clone) (@shawnmerwin) April 14, 2019' carries both halves: the streams point ('if boxed text worked well, then we would see it used on the streams as a go-to to start a scene. I don't think we ever see it. Instead, we see a back-and-forth between the DM & Players.') and Merwin's reply ('While this is true, different people (and roles) have different needs. A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully) to make their lives easier when they buy adventure content. So it is a risk not to provide what your audience and consumers want.'). The streams half reads as quoted-tweet text that Merwin accepts with 'While this is true'; the page attributes the whole blockquote to him. 'Publishers keep providing it' is carried by 'it is a risk not to provide what your audience and consumers want' — prudential rather than descriptive, but the causal link is his.

verdicts.trueWording: Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (HTTP 200). Two Merwin tweets on the page. Nov 23, 2021: 'This is exactly why boxed text is important. It's more than description. It's a series of prompts that can help your game flow more smoothly.' — quote-tweeting DM David's 'The quicker a description tempts players to act, the sooner DMs can stop talking and players can do something', which carries the push-players-toward-action limb. Nov 26, 2021: 'As a designer, I've found myself using boxed text to convey the atmosphere that I want to convey to the DM reading my adventure… it's over to them how they then convey that to their players. (Perhaps that's why I prefer to call it "narrative text"). Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting, and atmosphere is definitely part of that burden.' Quote matches word for word; only the sentence-initial E is capitalized on the page. (Sage Advice post date May 24, 2022; the claim's 2021-11 is the tweet dates.)

verdicts.trueWording: break it up into actionable chunks
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched direct (HTTP 200, no block, no Wayback needed); article dated August 1st, 2022, titled 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', on Justin Alexander's site (byline block 'JUSTIN ALEXANDER'; a commenter writes 'I also tend to agree with Justin's critiques'). Naming limb: 'Freeze-frame boxed text is when the GM starts reading and then the PCs are frozen in place while a bunch of stuff happens.' Advance-past-reaction limb: 'what you should avoid at all costs is having the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point without letting the players react'. Cure limb, verbatim: 'what you should do is break it up into actionable chunks' and 'The other actionable chunks are:'.

verdicts.trueWording: you have effectively removed from the game
verdicts.note: Same raw page. 'Remote-control boxed text suffers from similar problems (preventing the players from participating), but insidiously goes one step further by declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs.' Agency limb: 'When you take the one thing they control away from them — even for a little bit — you have effectively removed from the game. They are, in fact, no longer a player, but merely a spectator.' The quote is verbatim including the source's own dropped word ('removed from the game', missing 'them'). Forbidden limb: 'So… don't do this.' in an entry of the 'GM Don't List'.
